item.title: The world's top trade fair delivers opportunities from China to partners
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-15 00:05:00
Guests communicate before the opening ceremony of the 140th China Import and Export Fair (Canton Fair), held in Guangzhou, South China's Guangdong Province on October 14, 2026. Photo: CNS Photo Chinese President Xi Jinping on Wednesday sent a congratulatory letter to the 140th edition of the China Import and Export Fair, also known as the Canton Fair. In his letter, Xi said over the past 70 years since its establishment, the Canton Fair has played a significant role in promoting trade exchanges between China and other countries, serving as an effective platform for China to expand high-level opening up and promote the building of an open world economy. An opening ceremony for the 140th session was held on Wednesday. Chinese Premier Li Qiang attended the ceremony and delivered a keynote speech, emphasizing that China will continue to promote high-quality development, expand high-standard opening up, and take proactive and practical actions to add more impetus to the world economy. He said China stands ready to share more market opportunities, expand more mutually beneficial cooperation, and firmly safeguard the international economic and trade order with all parties. Participants at the opening ceremony, including representatives of exhibitors and buyers, echoed that the Canton Fair has grown into a significant trade platform for people from all over the world to match supply and demand. The 70-year journey of the Canton Fair is a vivid microcosm of China's transition from "selling to the world" to "linking the global supply chain." "I've been attending the Canton Fair for the last 10 years. It is always something very special for me, because every time I attend, I discover something new," Ahmed Abdelraouf Samman, general manager of SMN International, also a veteran participant from Egypt, told the Global Times on Wednesday. He characterized the Canton Fair as embodying innovation, credibility and a new world. "If you want to start any business, enhance your business, grow your business, or even take your business much farther, the Canton Fair is the place - all in one." For Rehman, director of social media services at RK Co, Ltd., the Canton Fair has provided a lot of business opportunities. The Pakistan-born participant has attended the Canton Fair for 10 years. "I grew up with the Canton Fair. I found many suppliers for different kinds of products at the fair, and we partner together to bring customized products to my customers in the Middle East market," Rehman told the Global Times. Continuous opening-up, more opportunities This year marks the 70th anniversary of the Canton Fair. From its inaugural session of just 9,600 square meters and 1,200 buyers in April 1957 to today's 1.55 million square meters and around 340,000 buyers, the fair has been held without interruption for 140 sessions. It serves as the most tangible proof of China's long-term commitment to opening-up. In 2007, at its 101st session, the Canton Fair was officially renamed the China Import and Export Fair, changing from its designation as the Chinese Export Commodities Exhibition. That was when it introduced an import section for the first time, shifting from a one-way export platform to two-way trade one. The fair later grew into an important platform for international trade cooperation, according to exhibitors and buyers from around the world. To date, the total number of overseas buyers attending the Canton Fair onsite and online has exceeded 10 million. In 2021, the Canton Fair was held both online and offline for the first time, fully opening to domestic buyers to help foreign exhibitors explore the China market during a time when global trade was impacted. The import section has continued to expand, with more than 1,7000 companies from over 100 countries and regions participating, including Fortune 500 companies. This section is full of stories about how overseas companies expand their global sales network through the Canton Fair. For example, Tek Seng, a PVC manufacturer from Malaysia, achieved its goal of "selling globally" through the fair. "About 10 years ago, we started with a small independent booth. The Canton Fair helped us discover global business opportunities," a representative of the company said previously. "The Chinese market offers big opportunities for Colombian and Latin American enterprises. I've lived in China for over 15 years, so I can testify how China has become a good partner of South America and Colombia," Juan Juan Camilo Basto, co-funder of Basal Trading Co, a member of the Colombian-Chinese Chamber of Investment and Commerce, told the Global Times on Wednesday. Basto has attended the Canton Fair 25 times. He described it as the "World Cup of the business," meaning it's the most important international business meeting. 'Factory of factories' Apart from providing a platform, the Canton Fair epitomizes how China's products, technologies and services are enabling global suppliers to upgrade and become more intelligent. Phase 1 of the 140th Canton Fair is themed "advanced manufacturing," featuring more than 25,000 booths and over 12,000 exhibitors. This phase showcases17 emerging future industry zones, including service robots, drones and display technology. Two exhibition halls highlight brain-computer interfaces, new energy storage, high-end chips and AI visualization products. These exhibits are not only the latest achievements of "Made in China" but also a window for "Chinese capabilities" to be exported to the world. China's exports of intermediate products - viewed as "Chinese capabilities" - provide essential support for production and exports in other countries, positioning China as a "factory of factories." This helps overseas factories achieve digital and intelligent upgrades through products and technology. "China plays an important role in the world, not only as a factory for producing goods, but also in adding value to the market - we can exchange knowledge and technologies," said Basto. Relying on the world's most complete industrial system, Chinese manufacturing has built a full-chain supply capacity, spanning from core components and high-end equipment to system solutions. This helps offset global industrial-chain fragmentation and supply-chain volatility. This strength is evident among exhibitors. Guangzhou-based industrial IoT platform provider iROOTECH has developed integrated software-hardware solutions through industrial intelligence and robotics, serving enterprises in more than 120 countries and regions. "Our intelligent after-sales maintenance platform helps our overseas customers solve the 'last mile' problem. For one of our customers in Thailand, the time required for fault detection and diagnosis was reduced by over 50 percent, maintenance efficiency increased by 30 percent, and losses from unplanned downtime were saved, amounting to more than 100 million yuan ($14.9 million)," Xu Zinan, sales director at iROOTECH, told the Global Times on Wednesday. This example shows how China is integrating into and supporting the global supply chain with a more open posture, not only providing goods to the world but also offering "manufacturing capability" itself. Advanced manufacturing and technology are becoming key forces that support the global supply chain. "From the perspective of the global supply chain, Chinese enterprises are a crucial part. In terms of markets, China's expanding market, which continues to open wider, offers more opportunities all over the world," Tian Yun, a Beijing-based economist, told the Global Times. At this 70th-anniversary milestone, the Canton Fair represents more than commodity trading. It symbolizes the certainty China offers the world: In an age of supply-chain fragmentation, advanced manufacturing and technological capabilities from China provide critical support for global stability, participants said.

item.title: India's 'victory narrative' will only hit a wall on China-India border: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-14 23:51:00
China, India Illustration: GT By changing a few place names, creating some media hype, it projects a tough stance and creates the illusion that its territorial claims have been realized on the ground. Such petty scheming is, at its core, nothing more than psychological victory in the absence of real gains - a manifestation of the self-deluding "victory narrative" embraced by some in India, now projected onto the China-India boundary issue. Some people in India are once again playing games with maps over the China-India border issue. Recently, India's Ministry of Home Affairs announced what it called the "standard names" for 28 locations in the so-called "Union Territory of Ladakh" and marked them on official Indian maps. Some of these locations lie in areas on the western sector of the China-India border that are under China's actual control. Including the 27 locations in China's Zangnan, Southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region, that India illegally renamed unilaterally in August this year, India has forcibly slapped an "Indian label" on 55 locations along the China-India border in just two months. This tactic is nothing new. First comes an administrative announcement, followed by the names being entered on official maps, and then repeated amplification through the media. The intent is not hard to discern: India hopes that, at minimal cost, it can gradually shape perceptions of the boundary issue among its own public and the international community, dressing up its unilateral claims as so-called "established facts." By changing a few place names, creating some media hype, it can project a tough stance and create the illusion that its territorial claims have been realized on the ground. Such petty scheming is, at its core, nothing more than psychological victory in the absence of real gains - a manifestation of the self-deluding "victory narrative" embraced by some in India, now projected onto the China-India boundary issue. Naming a place cannot directly create territorial sovereignty, and a map is no final ruling on territorial sovereignty. In 2019, India unilaterally amended its domestic laws, revoked relevant constitutional provisions, and announced the creation of the so-called "Union Territory of Ladakh," deliberately incorporating Chinese territory in the western sector of the China-India border into its own administrative jurisdiction. China made its opposition clear at the time, and its position has remained firm and consistent ever since. If a country could simply pass a law unilaterally declaring its neighbor's territory to be its own, there would be no need for countries around the world to negotiate their border disputes. They could settle everything from behind a desk by redrawing maps, issuing notices, and stamping official documents. So, India's actions are unacceptable and have no legal effect. The status quo along the Ladakh sector of the boundary is not a blank sheet of paper that can be altered at will. The western sector of the China-India border has historically belonged to China, and China possesses sovereignty over the relevant areas, including Aksai Chin region in Northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, and has ample historical and legal grounds for its claims. India's claims stem from illegal boundary demarcations inherited from the colonial era, which successive Chinese governments have never recognized. This is precisely why India's place-naming move, designed purely to assert sovereignty and expand its claims on maps, is fundamentally different from China's lawful standardization of place names in Zangnan. Chinese territory will not become Indian simply because India assigns it a name. Such wishful thinking does nothing to help resolve the China-India boundary issue properly. The boundary issue has a bearing on the overall relationship between the two countries, and New Delhi also frequently speaks of the situation on border areas. When Prime Minister Narendra Modi met with Chinese leader in September this year, he called on the two countries to jointly safeguard peace and tranquility in the border areas. Earlier, India's ambassador to China, Vikram Doraiswami, wrote in the Global Times that peace and tranquility along the China-India border would help promote partnership and cooperation between the two sides. If that is indeed the case, India should exercise greater restraint on issues of this kind rather than provoke tensions. Some Indian politicians are now keen to stage political shows over the border issue to divert attention from domestic problems and pander to nationalist sentiment. Such behavior will only erode mutual trust between the two, do nothing to resolve the dispute, and create fresh obstacles to the improving China-India relationship. Ultimately, the negative consequences will also be borne by India itself. For years, China and India have maintained communication through channels such as meetings between their special representatives on the boundary question, making sustained efforts to manage differences and advance negotiations. The hard-won peace and tranquility in border areas deserve to be jointly safeguarded. China and India are important neighbors, major developing countries, and representatives of emerging economies. Their relationship extends beyond the bilateral sphere and carries global and strategic significance. Greater cooperation between the two countries within multilateral frameworks, including the United Nations, BRICS, the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, and the G20, is vital to addressing global challenges and upholding international fairness and justice. India should work with China in the same direction and approach bilateral relations with a strategic vision and a long-term perspective, using the political wisdom of mutual respect and understanding to overcome disturbances. China's commitment to improving and developing relations with India remains unchanged. We urge India to act in the broader interests of bilateral relations, exercise prudence in both words and actions on the boundary issue, and follow the important understandings reached by the two countries' leaders. India should strictly honor the relevant agreements between the two sides and take concrete steps to create a favorable environment for improving and developing bilateral relations, rather than take actions that further complicate the boundary issue. No unilateral move to alter the status quo can shake China's firm resolve to safeguard its sovereignty and territorial integrity, nor can it change the objective facts long established by history and the realities on the ground.

item.title: GT Voice: How Asia could benefit from AI-driven expansion of trade
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-14 22:55:00
AI Illustration: Chen Xia/Global Times The IMF's new chief economist Silvana Tenreyro said on Tuesday that global trade grew 8.3 percent between 2023 and 2025, while global trade in AI grew by 29 percent, benefiting China, India and other Asian countries, Reuters reported. Why has Asia reaped the benefits of the expansion of AI trade? First, AI depends heavily on hardware. Chip manufacturing, server assembly, data center construction and power infrastructure all require a mature industrial system, large-scale manufacturing capacity and a stable supply chain network as their foundation. After decades of industrial upgrading and technological accumulation, the capacity and cost advantages in these segments have long been concentrated in Asia. From memory chip manufacturing to the ecosystem covering advanced processes, server components and cooling systems, to the large-scale production capacity of servers, optical modules and electronic components, Asia has formed the world's most complete AI hardware supply network. In the first eight months of this year, China's exports of servers, optical modules and electronic components grew at double-digit rates year-on-year, while its share of global humanoid robot shipments rose to 97 percent, according to customs statistics. Behind these figures lies the supply capacity that Asian manufacturing has unleashed in the AI hardware sector. Second is the scale effect on the demand side. China and India combined have more than 2.8 billion people, a regional market without parallel anywhere else in the world. It serves as both a vast proving ground for AI applications and a mega-buyer of AI hardware and services. In Asia, AI demand is being released simultaneously across countless scenarios, such as AI-assisted product selection for cross-border e-commerce livestreams, image recognition built into educational devices, and AI-powered quality inspection on factory floors. Feedback from hundreds of millions of users feeds back into product iteration at a speed unmatched elsewhere. This is what AI adoption in Asia looks like: not confined to laboratories or launch events, but reaching into every capillary of commerce, manufacturing and daily consumption. That endogenous demand is itself a key pillar of global AI trade. Some may be wondering whether Asia's deep participation in the AI cycle comes at the expense of advanced economies. The answer is no. Asia's AI-driven growth is not about taking dividends away from them. It is about making the global AI pie larger by providing manufacturing capacity and market space. Asian factories supply computing equipment to the world, and Asian markets provide revenue and users to global AI companies. The stable operation of Asian supply chains in turn supports the return expectations of global AI investment. This is a mutually reinforcing cycle, not a zero-sum game. The scale of this cycle is expanding rapidly. In recent years, global trade in AI-related products has grown far faster than overall merchandise trade. While AI-related goods may account for about 15 percent of world trade, trade in AI-enabling goods drove 42 percent of goods trade growth in 2025, and this share rose to 76 percent during the first quarter of 2026, according to World Trade Organization and Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development analysis. Without the large-scale, cost-effective AI hardware provided by Asian supply chains, the cost of global data center construction would rise sharply, the pace of AI adoption would be far slower, and AI deployment in every country would ultimately suffer. Conversely, the rapid growth of Asia's AI industry has also created substantial new import demand, from high-end research and development equipment to specialized software in niche fields to AI service solutions adapted to different markets. This does not mean Asia can rest easy. Challenges such as geopolitical disruptions to supply chains, export controls on critical technologies, and bottlenecks in power and computing infrastructure could all affect the sustainability of this round of dividends. But for now, with the region's ability to capture the dividends of AI trade expansion, Asia has already secured a key position on that track.

item.title: Takaichi's claim on nuclear policy wording 'conceals intent to dismantle postwar nuclear constraints'
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-14 22:49:00
Demonstrators stage a rally before the Diet in Tokyo, Japan, 21 November 2025. Nihon Hidankyo, the Japan Confederation of A-and H-Bomb Sufferers Organizations, and others political organizations and unions, staged a protest in front of the Japanese Parliament after the new Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi criticized her country's traditional policy against nuclear weapons. Photo: VCG Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi claimed on Wednesday there was room for discussion regarding the wording of the "no introduction" clause under Japan's Three Non-Nuclear Principles as Japan plans to revise its three key security documents by the end of this year, a move that has drawn concerns over whether Japan is seeking to loosen its long-standing nuclear policy constraints, a Chinese expert said. The expert noted the move is "an attempt to conceal its true intent" and reflects a dangerous signal that Japan is seeking to dismantle its postwar nuclear policy restrictions, which is unacceptable, and warned that any weakening of the "no introduction" principle could hollow out Japan's non-nuclear policy, open the door for US nuclear weapons to enter Japan, and bring risks to peace and stability in Northeast Asia. According to Japanese media TBS News, Takaichi made the claims at a meeting on Wednesday, saying that while the government is discussing the revision of the three security-related documents, the specific wording of the "no introduction" principle is still under consideration. She also referred to the concept of US extended deterrence, saying these issues deserved consideration, while declining to predict the final wording. This is not simply a consideration of review of wording, but an attempt to create room to dismantle Japan's postwar nuclear policy restrictions. It is an attempt to cover up the real intention, Lü Chao, a research fellow at the Liaoning Academy of Social Sciences, told the Global Times on Wednesday. Lü said that the so-called "review of wording" could become the first step toward gradually relaxing nuclear policy constraints, eventually hollowing out the non-nuclear policy that Japan has maintained for decades, adding that there should be no room for compromise on such an issue. "If even the key wording of this principle can be reinterpreted, the actual binding force of the Three Non-Nuclear Principles will be further weakened," the expert said. China's Foreign Ministry has previously stressed that the possession of nuclear weapons is not an issue on which Japan can "allow discussion" if it wants to. Japan is a non-nuclear-weapon state party to the Non-Proliferation Treaty and therefore has a bound duty under international law to not receive, manufacture, acquire or transfer nuclear weapons. There is no room for negotiation, a spokesperson said. Takaichi's moves toward revising the Three Non-Nuclear Principles has also already triggered many concerns among some groups in Japan for some time. Japanese Communist Party lawmaker Yoshiko Kira previously criticized the move, saying that instead of revising the principles against the wishes of atomic bomb survivors, Japan should join the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons, which she said was the responsibility of the only country to have suffered wartime atomic bombings, according to local media reports. Japan's Ryukyu Shimpo previously wrote in a commentary that revising the Three Non-Nuclear Principles would amount to abandoning Japan's postwar vision as a peace-oriented nation, saying that as the only country to have suffered atomic bombings, Japan should not weaken its non-nuclear commitments. Earlier this year, 22 civic groups in Nagasaki also issued a joint protest statement opposing any move to revise the principles, Mainichi reported. As Japanese right-wing forces keep challenging the postwar international order and the non-proliferation regime to move further down the wrong path, the international community needs to call on Japan to strictly observe the three non-nuclear principles, fulfill its obligations under the NPT, abandon remilitarization and nuclear attempt, and earnestly respond to the concerns of the international community, a Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson said. "Such a remilitarization trend will not only alter Japan's own security direction, but also intensify strategic competition in Northeast Asia and bring risks to regional peace and stability," Lü added.

item.title: Philippine military backs suspension of direct communication with China, raising risks of misjudgment, escalation: expert
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-14 22:02:00
Defense Secretary of the Philippines Gilbert Teodoro Jr. File photo: VCG The Philippine military has thrown its support behind Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr.'s suspension of direct military-to-military communication channels with China, as the Chinese Embassy in Manila warned that shutting down such contact fuels mistrust and narrows the space for crisis management amid continuing tensions in the South China Sea. The Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) claimed Tuesday that it "stands solidly behind and firmly supports" Teodoro's move, according to a report from the Philippine News Agency on Tuesday. A Chinese expert noted that the suspension of military-to-military communications between China and the Philippines would further undermine dialogue and mutual trust, while increasing the risk of misjudging each other's intentions. In the context of frequent maritime encounters, such miscalculations could severely weaken crisis management, raise the likelihood of sudden or unintended incidents, and expose frontline personnel on both sides to greater risks if tensions escalate unexpectedly because of less available communication channels. The AFP spokesperson, retired Rear Admiral Roy Vincent Trinidad, claimed communication mechanisms could only work when based on what he described as mutual trust, sincerity and support for international law. He claimed bilateral dialogue had failed because "the messages" did not match "the actions on sea, air and ground," and accused China of using direct communication as a "smokescreen," a report in the Philippine Star said on Wednesday. Trinidad also claimed that the AFP will continue to perform its sea patrol and "will keep performing rotation and resupply missions," according to the Philippine Star report. The Chinese Embassy in the Philippines, responding to the suspension, said "communication channels should remain open to avoid miscalculation and prevent tensions from escalating." The Embassy criticized Teodoro for shutting down military-to-military communication for "political self interests," warning that the move "fuels mistrust, narrows the space for crisis management, and pushes frontline personnel closer to confrontation," according to the Embassy's Facebook account. The current dispute indicates that the suspension did not begin this week. Coverage from Philippine-based media outlet the Daily Tribune said that Teodoro claimed on Tuesday that military-to-military communication with China had been suspended for nearly three years. In a May 2024 statement posted by the Philippine Department of National Defense, Teodoro said he had disallowed contact between the department and the Chinese Embassy since a courtesy call by then Chinese Ambassador Huang Xilian shortly after Teodoro took office in July 2023. Although China and the Philippines maintain other communication channels, they cannot fully replace direct military-to-military contact. Diplomatic channels are mainly used for broader policy and strategic coordination, while coast guard communication focuses more on specific maritime law enforcement. Military exchanges, by contrast, deal with more specialized and sensitive issues involving defense policy, military strategy and security concerns, Chen Xiangmiao, a research fellow at the National Institute for South China Sea Studies, told the Global Times on Wednesday. Chen noted that military communication serves as an important "backstop" for bilateral relations. Even when serious differences exist in the South China Sea, direct military contact can help clarify strategic intentions and security red lines, preventing specific maritime incidents from escalating into broader military confrontations. Given that the Philippine military also plays a role in planning and directing some maritime operations, restoring effective military-to-military communication remains important if Manila genuinely wants to manage disputes and reduce risks, Chen said. The latest military position comes as the Marcos administration stresses that the president intends to maintain engagement with Beijing. Palace communications undersecretary Claire Castro said that Manila would continue engaging with China, particularly in trade and investment, a report from News Watch Plus Philippines on Tuesday shows. Just days earlier, Marcos said his "greatest fear" was that a mistake by a seaman or soldier could develop into "something that goes out of control," while stressing the importance of managing problems and preventing misunderstandings in the South China Sea. The expert pointed out that the Philippine government's position appears to be internally inconsistent: while the presidential palace stresses dialogue and maintaining normal engagement with China, the defense establishment supports suspending direct military communication. Cutting such a channel would not make the Philippines safer, but would further weaken trust, increase the risk of miscalculation and ultimately impose greater security and political costs on Manila. Chen said this reflects a "double-track" approach: Manila portrays itself as willing to communicate and maintain overall bilateral stability, while continuing actions in the South China Sea that undermine existing understandings and create new friction. If the Philippines genuinely wants to manage risks, it should stop provocative actions, return to dialogue and restore effective crisis-management channels, including military-to-military communication.

item.title: China's foreign trade growth in first three quarters hits five-year high
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-14 21:37:00
Cargo vessels handle foreign trade containers at Lianyungang Port container terminal, East China's Jiangsu Province, in the early morning of October 14, 2026. Photo: CNS Photo China's total imports and exports reached 39.94 trillion yuan ($5.94 trillion) in the January-September period, soaring 18.8 percent year-on-year, marking the highest level for the same period in five years, data from the General Administration of Customs (GAC) showed on Wednesday. Chinese experts noted that these better-than-expected figures highlight the strong momentum of China's foreign trade, demonstrating the competitiveness and resilience of the country's manufacturing sector. Pushing back against Western media hype regarding the so-called expansion of China's trade surplus, these experts argued that rising trade protectionism, the overstretch of the national security concept and policy unpredictability - not China's surplus - are the factors that have widened global imbalances in recent years. These issues require joint efforts to resolve, rather than for pinning the blame on China, they stressed. Better-than-expected growth From January to September, China's exports increased by 16.4 percent year-on-year to 23.2 trillion yuan, while imports expanded by 22.3 percent to 16.74 trillion yuan, according to data released by the GAC. Foreign trade growth in the first three quarters was the fastest for the same period in the past five years, with both quarterly and monthly growth rates generally accelerating, said Wang Jun, GAC's deputy head. "Latest international data show that such a growth rate ranks among the top among major economies, and China remains the world's largest trader of goods," the official stated at a press conference on Wednesday. In September alone China's total imports and exports reached 5.16 trillion yuan, up 27.5 percent from a year earlier and crossing the 5-trillion-yuan mark for the first time. This figure also marked the sixth consecutive month of double-digit monthly growth. "Despite a complex and volatile external environment, China's trade in goods has sustained strong growth momentum - a testament to the solid backing of its comprehensive industrial system and the powerful boost from technological innovation," Tian Yun, a Beijing-based economist, told the Global Times. In the first three quarters, China's exports of integrated circuits (ICs) jumped by 99.1 percent, while computer parts and accessories tripled, and storage components, including Solid State Drives, more than doubled, ensuring a steady supply of intermediate goods for global computing power supply chains, data from the GAC showed. Meanwhile, the country's server exports rose by 7.2 percent, bolstering global computing infrastructure. AI glasses, biomimetic robots and other Chinese smart products are gaining traction overseas, broadening AI application scenarios worldwide. "China's exports have remained elevated for three main reasons. First, the ongoing global AI investment boom is fueling record growth in chip and related exports. Second, AI-driven global growth has outweighed the drag from the Middle East conflict, with external demand firming further in September and lifting export growth across the board. Third, years of manufacturing upgrading in China are paying off, visibly boosting exports of new energy vehicles and high-tech products," Feng Lin, an analyst with Orient Golden Credit Rating, wrote in a note sent to the Global Times. Strength rooted in competitiveness However, some Western media outlets - neglecting China's role as an anchor of stability for global industrial and supply chains - keep hyping up China's so-called "trade surplus." "Many of China's trading partners are facing weak growth prospects and are fearful of their manufacturing industries being overrun by exports from China," The Associated Press claimed in a report on Wednesday, citing an analyst. "Generally, trade surpluses tend to emerge in economies with robust manufacturing capacity," Wan Zhe, a professor at Beijing Normal University, told the Global Times. Deficit economies typically feature low savings, high consumption and fiscal deficits, which create financing gaps that have to be covered by external capital. Surplus economies display the opposite pattern, Wan noted, adding that the shifting landscape of surplus nations reflects the relocation of manufacturing capacity - this is driven by economic realities of industrial migration, rather than deliberate policy choices alone. The rising trade protectionism, the overstretching of the concept of national security and policy unpredictability are key factors contributing to worsening global imbalances in recent years, Wan said, noting that addressing such imbalances requires countries to advance their own structural reforms. = Committed to promoting balanced trade growth, China has intensified efforts to expand imports this year. According to the GAC, China's imports rose by 22.3 percent in the first three quarters of this year, with the growth rate exceeding 20 percent for seven straight months since March. In September, the country's monthly imports broke the 2 trillion yuan mark for the first time. Co-op opportunities Looking ahead, China's foreign trade prospects are bright. Against a backdrop of frequent disruptions to global supply chains and rising energy and geopolitical risks, China - with its comprehensive industrial system and stable, smoothly functioning supply capacity - is becoming a reliable anchor for the global market, Tian said. "We continue to expand market access. Since the beginning of this year, we have granted market access to hundreds of agri-food products, including bananas from Myanmar, corn from Pakistan and apples from Belgium. We have successfully held eight editions of the China International Import Expo (CIIE), which has attracted a cumulative 27,000 exhibitors from more than 180 countries and regions, with intended transaction volume exceeding $580 billion. The CIIE provides a premium platform for quality products from around the world to better access the Chinese market," Wang said. At the upcoming ninth CIIE to be held in Shanghai next month, a wide array of cutting-edge and hard-tech products will debut. To support the event, China's customs authority has rolled out 18 facilitation measures spanning the entire process - from exhibit import and customs supervision to post-exhibition handling. This includes a new provision allowing bonded goods in bonded warehouses to be displayed after a guarantee is provided. These concrete measures are designed to help more quality products access the Chinese market. "With all restrictions on foreign investment in the manufacturing sector now fully removed and national treatment for foreign-invested enterprises steadily ensured, we are confident that more foreign companies will choose to deepen their roots in China - achieving mutual success and growing together with Chinese firms, and sharing the dividends of 'China Opportunity 2.0,'" Wang said.

item.title: First China-Pakistan army joint training features an all-Chinese equipment lineup, signaling deep interoperability: expert
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-14 21:19:00
Image of the opening ceremony of the China-Pakistan Karakoram 2026 joint army training held at a training base in Korla, Northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region Photo: Screenshot from the CCTV's military channel The first China-Pakistan army joint training Karakoram 2026 kicked off on Wednesday, with all weapons and equipment provided by the Chinese side, China Central Television's (CCTV) military channel reported. A military affairs expert said the choice of medium-weight wheeled vehicles for high-altitude operations, and Pakistan's use of an all-Chinese lineup, signal deepening military trust and potential future procurement. The opening ceremony for the China-Pakistan Karakoram 2026 joint army training was held at a training base in Korla, Northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region. It is the first army joint training between the two countries, themed on joint counter-terrorism and clearance operations in high-altitude areas, said the report. The report said that all weapons and equipment in the training were provided by China, including Type 191 rifles, Type 201 squad machine guns, Type 11 armored assault vehicles, Type 08 infantry fighting vehicles, as well as artillery, unmanned and anti-unmanned systems. Wang Yunfei, a military affairs expert, told the Global Times on Wednesday that the two types of vehicles are both wheeled platforms. In high-altitude areas, wheeled armored vehicles have their own advantages. Unlike tracked vehicles, they are faster, especially during road maneuvers, and easier to maintain, making them well-suited for movement and combat missions on the plateau. The all-Chinese equipment lineup covers multiple categories and forms a relatively complete combat system, he said. On one hand, it shows China has provided weapons and equipment technology to Pakistan. On the other hand, these weapons could be procured by Pakistan in future military trade, further expanding the presence of Chinese equipment in the Pakistan Army. This joint training thus serves as a rehearsal and a process of familiarization. From a broader perspective, it also reflects strategic mutual trust, showing that military cooperation between the two countries has reached a high level. Building this kind of deep interoperability will lay a solid foundation for future joint operations between the two armies in counter-terrorism, border control and other areas, the expert said. Zhang Jueshe, another military affairs expert, told the Global Times that China and Pakistan complement each other well in the field of counter-terrorism, while cooperation can be advanced via intelligence sharing, joint operations, technology transfers, experience exchanges and economic cooperation. "China could provide Pakistan with technical and equipment support, including drones and smart combat platforms, to boost its surveillance and early warning capacity against terrorist groups, and also conduct experience training," he noted. Pakistan's experience in addressing complex border security situations, handling local separatist forces and coordinating counter-terrorism efforts can also provide references for China to tackle similar non-traditional security challenges, Zhang added. On Saturday, Senior Colonel Chen Xi, a spokesperson for the Chinese Ministry of National Defense, announced that in mid- and late October, Chinese and Pakistani armies will hold Karakoram 2026 joint army training in Korla, Xinjiang. Focusing on joint counter-terrorism operations in high-altitude areas, the activity will include skills training in UAV operation, on-the-move target search and firing, and long-range sniping, and cover joint command and live-force exercises. The exercise will expand the scope of China-Pakistan military cooperation, reflect growing mutual trust, and strengthen counter-terrorism collaboration through the sharing of experience and expertise, Zhang said.

item.title: Europe, beware of Taiwan politician's self-serving 'warning'
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-14 21:02:00
China-EU relationship Photo: VCG Certain forces of the Taiwan region are exploiting yet another international platform to peddle their separatist agenda, this time using a Western buzzword in Poland to drag the EU into its political stunts. According to media reports, Taiwan's "foreign minister" Lin Chia-lung, during a speech in Poland on Tuesday, warned the EU that dependence on Chinese suppliers poses a risk to the bloc's freedom. The remarks came as European leaders will gather in Brussels this week to weigh up the future of trading ties with China. Such remarks serve a number of ulterior motivations behind Taiwan politicians. First, Taiwan politicians harbor no genuine concern for the EU's interests, but only want to internationalize the Taiwan question by hijacking a major China-EU agenda, creating the false impression that Taiwan has a legitimate stake in Europe's trade and security decisions. Second, they aim to drive a wedge between China and the EU, exploiting Europe's internal debates on "de-risking" to sow suspicion and friction where none need exist. Third, they attempt to dress up a separatist agenda in the language of "freedom" and "values," borrowing Western slogans to lend their cause a veneer of legitimacy it does not deserve. After all, the one-China principle is a consensus of the international community and a norm governing international relations. As an inalienable part of China, Taiwan has no right - under any name, in any capacity, or on any international occasion - to issue so-called "warnings" or make pronouncements on China-EU relations. The EU's approach to China today is marked by a deep and unresolved ambivalence. On one hand, Brussels acknowledges the necessity of a "stable and balanced" trade relationship, recognizing that China remains an indispensable partner for Europe's economic and green transition goals. On the other hand, European institutions increasingly frame China as a "critical long-term strategic challenge," claiming it holds "asymmetric advantages" over the EU through its economic and technological dominance. Interdependence, once seen as a foundation for stability, is now treated as a source of vulnerability. This tension has driven the EU toward a policy of "de-risking," which in practice often looks less like prudent diversification and more like a deliberate effort to reduce dependence on Chinese suppliers across critical sectors. A case in point is that in June, the European Commission decided to propose a new law requiring EU companies to diversify their sources of key supplies, the focus of which, clearly, is China. With such measures as their policy tools, the EU is not protecting its freedom; it is eroding the very foundation of its prosperity. China has consistently supported a strong, united, and prosperous Europe. But if Brussels chooses to define its relationship with China through the lens of suspicion and adversarial posturing, it will find that the costs of derisking far outweigh the imagined risks of engagement. The timing of the so-called warning from the Taiwan politician is telling. It also came just days after EU and Chinese trade officials concluded their second Trade and Investment Consultations in Beijing, where both sides reached agreements on hybrid vehicle exports, rare earth supply channels, and market access. The EU should realize that the "warning" from Taiwan is nothing but a wolf in sheep's clothes. If European institutions allow such remarks to fester unchecked, or worse, use them as a pretext to advance the so-called "supply chain de-risking" agenda, it would mark a dangerous shift in Europe's trade policy - moving away from pragmatic cooperation and toward ideological confrontation. Such a move would only lend credibility to a separatist narrative that has no place in international affairs. If Brussels truly values strategic autonomy, it should resist the temptation to convert trade policy into an instrument of ideological posturing, and instead keep the China-EU relationship anchored in realism, reciprocity, and respect.

item.title: China launches eight new satellites to advance space-based AI computing network
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-14 20:15:00
Photo: Courtesy of Landspace China's plan to build a 2,800-satellite AI computing constellation in space took another step forward on Wednesday, as eight computing satellites were successfully launched into orbit to test technologies for AI model training, high-speed data transmission and advanced cooling technologies in space. The satellites, developed by Chinese space AI company ADA Space, were among 10 spacecraft aboard a commercial Zhuque-2E Y4 carrier rocket from the Dongfeng commercial space innovation pilot zone in Northwest China at around 7:40 pm on Wednesday, mission insiders told the Global Times. The launch marked the 10th flight of the Zhuque-2 rocket series, developed by Chinese commercial aerospace company LandSpace, and added to China's efforts to develop space-based computing infrastructure capable of supporting AI applications both in orbit and on Earth. The eight satellites are from the first batch of the second group under ADA Space's "Star Compute" program, which envisions a constellation of 2,800 computing satellites, including 2,400 dedicated to AI inference and 400 to AI training. The latest mission follows an earlier demonstration on how space-based computing could support applications on Earth. In April 2026, ADA Space announced that a system using AI models running aboard orbiting satellites to remotely control ground-based intelligent agents had passed 19 technical tests conducted by the China Academy of Information and Communications Technology. Building on these earlier advances, the newly launched satellites will undertake a new round of in-orbit experiments, including training AI foundation models in space, high-speed laser communications and advanced cooling technologies. These experiments will explore key technologies needed to build a larger and more interconnected orbital computing network, ADA Space said in a statement sent to the Global Times on Wednesday. Unlike conventional satellites that primarily collect data and transmit it back to Earth for processing, computing satellites are designed to perform complex calculations directly in orbit, potentially reducing dependence on ground-based data centers and enabling faster processing of space-generated information. According to ADA Space, the newly launched satellites carry high-performance computing payloads, laser communication equipment and Earth observation instruments. Among the most significant planned experiments is the training of AI foundation models directly in space, representing a further step beyond deploying previously trained AI models aboard satellites. The satellites will also test a 10-kilowatt-class liquid cooling system and large deployable radiator panels. These technologies are essential for managing the substantial heat generated by high-performance computing equipment in the vacuum of space. Unlike terrestrial data centers, which can use air circulation to dissipate heat, computing facilities in orbit must rely heavily on thermal radiation to release excess heat into space. Another major focus is the development of an interconnected laser communication network, allowing satellites to exchange large volumes of data at high speeds and potentially enabling computing resources to be coordinated across multiple spacecraft. The latest launch builds on China's earlier progress in developing space-based computing infrastructure. In May 2025, ADA Space launched the first group of satellites under its "Star Compute" program. In November 2025, the company announced that it had successfully deployed the Qwen3 large language model aboard its orbiting computing satellites, demonstrating progress in operating general-purpose AI models in space. These developments reflect a broader ambition to move beyond processing data collected in space and explore how orbital computing resources can also serve applications on Earth. Under the company's roadmap, a network of approximately 1,000 satellites is expected to be deployed and enter commercial operation before 2030, with the full constellation targeted for completion before 2035. In addition to the eight computing satellites, Wednesday's mission also carried two experimental laser communication satellites developed by Lanta Intelligent, which will test high-speed laser data transmission, integrated onboard processing and advanced solar power systems. The company previously launched two experimental satellites in November 2024, which have since conducted laser communication and flexible solar array technology demonstrations. Wednesday's mission came just 29 days after LandSpace's previous Zhuque-2E launch, reflecting efforts to increase launch frequency in China's commercial aerospace sector. Ma Haijing, a LandSpace spokesperson, told the Global Times that the company has adopted parallel mission preparations, coordinated production schedules and standardized launch procedures to improve launch efficiency while maintaining strict quality control. As China accelerates the development of satellite internet and space-based AI infrastructure, the ability to deploy multiple satellites efficiently is becoming increasingly important. The successful launch adds another eight computing satellites to China's expanding space-based AI infrastructure. Subsequent in-orbit testing will help assess progress toward putting a large-scale space computing network into practical use, ADA Space said.

item.title: HYROX postpones Shanghai event over venue issues following a Beijing race hygiene controversy
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-14 20:00:00
Joanna Wietrzyk of Australia in action during the HYROX Beijing event at the National Speed Skating Oval in Beijing, China, on September 12, 2026. Photo: VCG Indoor fitness competition HYROX announced on Wednesday that its Shanghai event would be postponed because of unforeseen problems with venue arrangements. The indoor hybrid fitness endurance race had previously faced attention after a competitor experienced a bowel incident mid-race at HYROX Beijing. The HYROX Shanghai event, originally scheduled for October 31 to November 1, 2026, will be postponed, the organizer said on its official Sina Weibo account. The venue will remain unchanged. All purchased race entries and spectator tickets will automatically be transferred to the rescheduled event dates. Those unable to attend the rescheduled event may apply for a full refund, the organizer said. The HYROX China organizing committee apologized to athletes and spectators for postponing the Shanghai event, acknowledging that the decision had disrupted their training and travel plans. On September 12, Australian athlete Joanna Wietrzyk experienced bowel incontinence during the women’s pro race at the HYROX Beijing event, held at the National Speed Skating Oval in Beijing. She continued competing and won the women’s pro race. The incident sparked online criticism over its impact on racecourse hygiene, as well as questions about the organizers’ sanitation measures and on-site management. Several athletes withdrew from the HYROX Shanghai event following the bowel incontinence controversy at the Beijing event, citing concerns over hygiene and safety at future races. Some withdrawing athletes filed lawsuits over refund processing fees, Chao News, a media outlet under Zhejiang Daily, reported in September. Global Times
